Abstract 
 
With the growing interest in sustainable manufacturing, 3D printing with recycled Polyethylene 
Terephthalate (rPET) offers an innovative approach to upcycling waste. This study explores 
the potential of combining rPET with milled short carbon fibres and polymer chain extenders to 
produce high-performance 3D printing filaments through melt extrusion. Filaments containing 
5% and 10% carbon fibre, with and without sizing, along with a polymer chain extender, were 
investigated to enhance viscosity and material properties of rPET. Thermal analysis techniques 
evaluated the material's thermal stability and transitions, assessing the degradation 
temperature and calorimetric properties including glass transition and melting temperatures, 
while the measured carbon fibre content closely matched the theoretical content. Tensile 
testing of unidirectionally printed samples showed promising mechanical properties. X-ray 
micro-computed tomography assessed fibre length in extruded filaments, comparing it with the 
target length set during manufacturing, showing agreement. Scanning electron microscopy 
examined fracture and side surfaces, revealing governing failure mechanisms and defects, 
attributed to filament production and composition. This study highlights the synergistic role of 
carbon fibre sizing and chain extenders in enhancing tensile modulus, while improving overall 
consistency and quality of extruded filaments. It presents a groundbreaking pathway for 
sustainable, high-performance additive manufacturing.

1. Introduction 
 
Between year 1950 and 2015, more than 8 billion tons of plastics have been manufactured 
globally, with the majority being sourced from non-renewable fossil fuels 1. Out of all the plastics 
produced, Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) is one of the major groups. It is commonly used 
for packaging, water bottles, and textile applications, due to its excellent thermal and 
mechanical properties 2,3. PET exhibits a high melting point of over 250°C, thermal conductivity 
ranging from 0.15 to 0.24 W/m/K, and a density of 1.38 g/cm³ at 20°C, which contribute to its 
suitability for such applications 4. Given its excellent physical and chemical properties 5, the 
production and consumption of PET have skyrocketed 6,7. This rise in demand is accompanied 
by enormous waste streams, which has raised the concern about the environmental impact of 
PET. Due to the inherent durability and long decomposition time of petroleum-based plastics8, 
like PET, many manufacturers and research institutions are turning to recycling as a key 
strategy to address the substantial waste streams generated 9. The physical and chemical 
properties of polymers arise from a complex interplay of factors, including intra- and 
intermolecular interactions, and characteristics such as molecular weight, and the 
polydispersity 10. Literature reports have expressed how thermal transitions are affected by the 
limited flexibility of the PET chain, which is due to the presence of the short ethylene group and 
the p-phenylene group 11,12. Thermal analysis techniques such as Thermogravimetric Analysis 
(TGA) and Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) are valuable tools for studying the thermal 
stability and transition behaviour of polymer-based materials. 
 
In recent years, the Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) technology has emerged as a promising 
method for incorporating recycled thermoplastics into the production of 3D-printed parts. 
Various types of waste thermoplastics, such as Polylactic Acid (PLA), Acrylonitrile Butadiene 
Styrene (ABS), Polypropylene (PP), and PET, can be recycled and used as raw materials for 
FFF 13. By converting these waste-derived materials into feedstock for FFF, manufacturers can 
reduce their reliance on virgin plastics and promote a circular economy, where materials are 
reused and repurposed. As interest in sustainable manufacturing grows, FFF offers a practical 
solution for transforming plastic waste into valuable products, addressing environmental 
concerns while also meeting the material demand in manufacturing.  
 
Printing with FFF using recycled thermoplastics offers a great opportunity, as it allows complex 
parts to be made and provides a way to upcycle thermoplastics. However, these end products 
often lack mechanical performance and do not have the desired structural integrity, which limits 
their applications to rapid prototyping 14,15. To address this issue, the thermoplastic feedstock 
is strengthened with reinforcements such as fibres 16 or particulates 17. To improve circularity 
even further, the reinforcement materials can also be recycled—for example, using recycled 
short glass fibre as reinforcement for PP 18, or recycled carbon fibre for PLA 19. In the particular 


 
 
case of PET, Katalagarianakis et al. 20 explored using recycled PET reinforced with recycled 
carbon fibre as feedstock and found significant improvements in terms of stiffness and strength 
in the FFF-printed sample. 
 
To enhance the mechanical properties of recycled thermoplastics, both external 
reinforcements and intrinsic modifications can be applied 15. One effective method is adding a 
chain extender, which increases the polymer's molar mass. As the molar mass increases, the 
mechanical properties of the thermoplastic improve 20. For instance, Zhao et al. 21 found that 
introducing a trifunctional chain extender to PET enhanced its tensile strength while reducing 
its crystallinity. Similarly, Makkam et. Al reported that blending PET with an acrylic epoxy resin 
chain extender also increased tensile strength and decreased crystallinity 22. Chain extenders 
not only increase the molar mass but also improve printability in fused filament fabrication. 
Diederichs et al. 23 observed that adding a chain extender to poly-trimethylene terephthalate 
produced filaments with superior diameter uniformity and reduced warping in printed parts. 
Another important factor in composite materials is the surface treatment or sizing of carbon 
fibres, which enhances adhesion with the matrix and protects the fibres during manufacturing. 
In a study by Ozkan et al.24, polycarbonate (PC) composites reinforced with both sized and 
unsized short carbon fibres were compared. The results showed that sized carbon fibre 
reinforced PC composites had higher tensile strength and modulus than unsized ones. 
Similarly, the interfacial shear strength (IFSS) of polyamide 6 (PA6) composites was tested 
with both sized and unsized carbon fibres 25. Fibre sizing refers to a surface treatment applied 
to carbon fibres, typically involving a thin coating or chemical agent, designed to improve 
adhesion between the fibre and the polymer matrix, enhancing the mechanical performance 
and durability of the composite material. C. Yan et al. found that treating carbon fibres with a 
sizing agent increased the IFSS by more than 20%. 
 
While numerous studies have investigated the recycling of PET and its reinforcement with 
fibres or additives, several key challenges persist. The inconsistent mechanical properties of 
rPET composites when used in fused filament fabrication (FFF), have limited their applications 
to mainly rapid prototyping, though they could potentially be utilized in other areas. While 
previous research has highlighted the potential of short carbon fibers and additives to enhance 
rPET’s mechanical properties, the interaction and combined effects of these modifications—
especially in the realm of 3D printing—remain insufficiently investigated. Most studies have 
limited their focus to singular modifications rather than exploring their synergy. To address this 
gap, a series of experiments were done to evaluate the thermal stability and microstructural 
characteristics of the extruded filaments. Tensile testing was employed to assess the 
mechanical properties of 3D printed samples, while thermal analysis provided insights into 
material stability. To further explore the internal structure, X-ray micro-computed tomography 
was used, complemented by scanning electron microscopy to observe fracture surfaces and 
failure mechanisms at a microstructural level. By addressing critical aspects such as fibre 
orientation, adhesion to the matrix, and the consistency of mechanical properties, this work 
aims to demonstrate how the synergistic effects of these modifications can elevate the 
performance of rPET composites for additive manufacturing, paving the way for broader 
industrial applications. 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Materials 
 
This study employed recycled materials for filament production, specifically recycled PET 
(rPET), recycled milled short carbon fibre (rCF), and polymer chain extender (viscosity 
booster). The rPET was acquired in the form of mechanically recycled flakes from Agfa-
Gevaert. According to Costa et al. 26, rPET exhibits a glass transition temperature of 72.2°C, a 
melt flow index (MFI) of 112.4 g/10 min—which is significantly higher than that of virgin PET—
and a cold crystallization temperature of 128.4°C. Increased MFI can improve processability in 
applications such as injection moulding, but it can also lead to defects in components when 
excessively high. Excessively high MFI may compromise mechanical properties or surface 
quality due to reduced intermolecular chain entanglement, which is critical for part strength and 
stability in additive manufacturing.  Procotex supplied regularly sized carbon fibres (CF MLD 
100) and unsized carbon fibres (CF LS MLD 100). It is important to note that in this study, the 
term "sizing" refers to the surface coating on the carbon fibre and is not related to the 
dimensions of the fibres. It is applied to protect the fibre from breaking during processing and 
to enhance their compatibility with the resin. According to the product technical datasheet, the 
regularly sized fibres have a sizing content of approximately 1.4 ± 0.6% weight percent, while 
the unsized fibres have less than 0.1%. Both fibre types have lengths ranging from 80 μm to 
100 μm with a diameter of 7 μm. The chain extender (CE) used was pelletised NEXAMITE 
M021200 from Nexam Chemical 27. 
 
2.2. Compounding and filament extrusion 
 
The rPET flakes, either unmodified or mixed with rCF and/or M021200, were processed on a 
Leistritz micro-27/GL-44D twin screw compounder and converted into pellets. The 
reinforcements and additives were blended with rPET during compounding. The feedstock 
filaments were produced by compounding and melt extrusion because it showed superior 
mechanical properties during the preliminary testing of the material. A die with a circular 
opening of 5 mm in diameter was used. The applied temperature profile ranged from 230°C to 
265°C, chosen to minimise the risk of thermal degradation. The extruder speed varied between 
220 and 222 rpm. The extruded strands were cooled in a water bath and pelletized to granules 
with a SGS 50-E type granulator. Melt spinning of the produced compounds was performed on 
a tailormade filament extrusion line of FET (Fiber Extrusion Technologies) as shown in Figure1. 
This pilot line is equipped with two extruders (throughput up to 6 kg/h), a water bath, three sets 
of drawing rolls with intermediate ovens and a set of relaxation rolls. A diameter control device 
(Laser 2005 XY combined with Ecocontrol 600, Sikora AG) was placed between the water bath 
and the first set of drawing rolls to monitor the thickness and roundness of the filament 
throughout the process. All produced filaments have a target diameter of 1.75 mm. The groups 
selected have predefined carbon fibre volume fractions of 5% and 10%. The composition for 
each filament group is detailed in Table 1. Note that filament made with 100 % rPET flake is 
not processable without additives due to reduced viscosity and unpredictable melt flow. These 
are the inherent consequences of the recycling process, where breakdown of polymer 
macromolecular chains occurs due to thermal and mechanical stresses during processing.

2.3. Thermal characterisation 
 
TGA was performed to determine the degradation temperature and the residue percentage. 
The test employed a heating rate of 10 °C.min-1 with all samples heated from 35°C to 750°C 
under nitrogen atmosphere. The TA Instrument Q50 was used, and the TGA results were 
analysed using the TA Universal Analysis software. 
 
DSC was performed on rPET flakes and filaments with a TA instrument DSCQ1000. The tests 
consist of two heating runs and a cooling run in between, with a temperature range of 0°C to 
325°C. The tests were conducted in a nitrogen atmosphere employing a heating and cooling 
rate of 10 °C·min-1. Glass transition temperatures (T𝑔,1, T𝑔,2) and melting temperatures (T𝑚,1, 
T𝑚,2) are determined from each heating run. The cold crystallisation temperature (T𝑐𝑐) is 
exclusively obtained from the first heating run. The cooling run provides information on the 
crystallisation temperature (T𝐶 ). The initial degree of crystallinity (XC1) of the filaments is 
computed using Equation 1.

2.4. Carbon fibre characterisation 
 
TGA, Optical Microscopy (OM) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) were conducted on 
the two groups of rCF. TGA was performed to verify the fibre content. Under a nitrogen 
atmosphere, the fibres were heated from 35°C to 750°C at a heating rate of 10 °C·min-1. TRIOS 
from TA instruments was used to analyse the resulting thermograms. To determine the initial 
length of the rCF, optical microscopy was adopted where 50 fibres from each fibre group were 
measured for their length. The optical microscope used was a Nikon eclipse LV100POL and 
post processing software. The surface morphology, roughness, and presence of sizing for each 
group of fibres were inspected using SEM, type JEOL JSM-7600F. The scans of carbon fibre 
reinforced rPET filaments were conducted using the custom-built HECTOR scanner 29 at the 
Ghent University Centre for X-ray Tomography (UGCT). The reconstruction software Octopus 
Reconstruction was used to reconstruct the 3D volume at an isotropic voxel size of 3 µm. The 
resulting images were processed using a custom code in Python as described in 20. 
 
2.5. Fused filament fabrication 
 
The extruded filaments were stored in ambient atmosphere at room temperature. Before 
printing they were dried for 24 hours at 30°C 30. After that, they were stored in a dry-box. These 
filaments were utilized for printing tensile samples using a Prusa i3 MK3S FFF printer, shown 
in Figure 2, with the specific settings outlined in Table 2. The tensile samples adhere to a 
dimension of 165 x 20 x 2.5 mm³, following the geometry specified in the ASTM D3039 
standard but with a reduced length due to the limitations in print bed size. The printing direction 
of the sample aligns parallel to the load direction of the tensile test, denoted as 0°. The selection 
of 3D printing parameters in this study was carefully determined based on the characteristics 
of the rPET filament and the requirement for high-quality tensile specimens. The nozzle 
temperature was set at 275 °C to ensure proper melting and flow of the filament, minimizing 
defects such as under-extrusion. A build plate temperature of 100 °C was chosen to reduce 
warping and shrinkage during the printing process. To balance productivity and print quality, a 
print speed of 40 mm/s was selected, with an initial speed for the first layer set lower than 
subsequent layers to ensure better adhesion to the print bed, reducing the risk of warping or 
detachment during the printing process. The 0.1 mm layer height ensures high dimensional 
accuracy and surface quality for tensile specimens, minimizing stress concentrators and 
variability during mechanical testing.

2.6. Mechanical testing 
 
The mechanical properties of the printed samples were assessed using tensile tests, with five 
samples tested for each material composition. An Instron 5885 electromechanical testing 
system equipped with pneumatic side action grips and a 10 kN load cell were employed for the 
tests. As prescribed by the standard in ASTM D3039/D3039M-08 31, displacement control at a 
crosshead displacement rate of 2 mm/min was adopted for all tensile tests. The dimensions of 
each sample were measured using a calliper before testing. The strain was measured with an 
Instron 2630-100 dynamic extensometer featuring a gauge length of 50 mm. Young’s moduli 
of the samples were determined between a strain of 0.1% and 0.3%. One-way ANOVA was 
used to calculate significant differences (p<0.05). Mechanically tested samples underwent 
examination of their fracture surfaces using SEM to analyse the failure mode, apparent defects, 
and fibre-matrix bonding behaviour in the printed samples. 
 
 
 


 
 
3. Results and discussion 
 
3.1. Thermal characterisation 
 
The thermal degradation behaviour of each filament group was analyzed using TGA to assess 
the material's stability and the effects of CF content, sizing, and chain extenders on degradation 
characteristics. In Table 3, the residual percentages and the corresponding CF content are 
presented. The residue consists of carbonized material consisting of both rPET and CF. To 
estimate the CF percentage in a specimen, the rPET residue is subtracted from the total 
residue mass. This step is critical for isolating the thermal contribution of CF from the polymer 
matrix and establishing how the inclusion of additives modifies the overall behaviour. To 
establish a benchmark for the rPET residue, two groups were introduced: rPET3CE and 
DCVKC, being an extruded rPET with chain extenders, and rPET pellets, respectively. The 
results indicated a direct correlation between CF content and residue percentage, as higher 
CF percentages resulted in increased residue. This observation is consistent with the known 
thermal stability of CF, where under an inert atmosphere, it undergoes minimal oxidation and 
exhibits negligible mass loss 32 up to a 1000 °C.  CF remains intact provided that the 
temperature is below 750 °C.  Despite the difference in the residue percentage, the degradation 
onset temperature (T𝑑,𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒𝑡 ) remains consistent, falling in between 395 °C and 400 °C, 
suggesting that neither CF content nor additives significantly influence the initial thermal 
decomposition of the composite. This aligns with the findings of Katalagarianakis et al 20, further 
corroborating that the primary degradation mechanism is governed by the polymer matrix 
rather than the reinforcement phase.

Figures 3 and 4 provide a comprehensive visualization of the degradation trends. Below 350°C, 
the analysis of the thermograms reflects stability as shown in Figure 3, followed by a rapid 
degradation process associated with the simultaneous breaking of both ester and aliphatic 
moieties 33–35. The thermograms were used to determine the CF content (as described above), 
which was then compared to the theoretical values defined prior to filament production. The 
bottom lines in the plot refer to groups rPET3CE and DCVKC without carbon fibres. The 
behaviour of the two groups with no CF and the drop in residue percentage are consistent, 
where an overlap in the plots is observed. Observing Figure 3, a magnified view of the 
thermograms is presented, focusing on the residue at the end of the TGA test, highlighting the 
residue trends and reinforcing the quantitative results. This comparison clearly illustrates the 
trend confirmed by the quantitative results shown in Table 3. As the CF content increases, 
there is a corresponding rise in the residue percentage. This increased percentage indicates 
the presence of residue, given the testing conditions and CF decomposition temperature 


 
 
threshold, while this residue highlights the remaining intact carbon fibre. Additionally, the 
groups containing sizing and chain extenders consistently yielded lower residue than the 
groups without.

and rPET recycled with different CF percentages, with and without chain extender. 
 
To better observe the differences, four groups are shown in Figure 4. The groups chosen are 
with different CF% content, with and without chain extenders. The groups with 5% CF content 
clearly show a lower residue percentage on the plot. As anticipated, the groups with 10% CF 
reflect an increased residue. In addition, the groups with chain extender yield roughly 1% lower 
residue content at the end of the tests.  The chain extender, acting as a catalyst, can interact 
with reinforcement fillers, alter the thermal decomposition pathway of the material and enhance 
the breakdown of the polymer chains at lower temperatures, reducing the amount of residue 
36,37. It might improve the oxidative stability of the material, resulting in a lower residue at the 
end of the TGA analysis 38. The results emphasize that the thermal degradation process is not 
solely dictated by the reinforcement but is a composite interaction involving matrix additives. 
Furthermore, the distinction between groups with and without sizing was evident from the 
residue percentages. Referring to Figure 3, it is evident that the plots of groups with sizing 
show a lower residue percentage compared to unsized, and the quantitative results in Table 3 
show this difference to be approximately 0.2 - 0.5%. The presence of sizing slightly increases 
the overall density of the composite, and as the sizing burns off during the analysis, the 
remaining carbon fibre residue appears lower in proportion compared to the unsized group, 
where only pure carbon fibre remains. This difference, although minimal, underscores the 
importance of precise characterization when additives are involved. These results, along with 
further quantitative analysis, were used to evaluate the achieved CF content and determine 
how closely it aligns with the theoretical CF, as presented in figure 5.

To examine the influence of additives on the thermal behaviour of each filament group, DSC 
was conducted, and the results are presented in Table 4. This thermoanalytical technique helps 
characterizing material properties by detecting endothermic and exothermic transitions in the 
samples. Glass transitions are identified by the inflection point in the baseline, while melting 
points and crystallization are depicted by endothermic and exothermic peaks, respectively 39–
41. The DSC analysis complements the TGA findings by exploring the thermal transitions and 
crystallinity changes induced by additives. 
Polymer fibre bonding significantly affects crystallinity. Sizing has been shown to enhance the 
interfacial adhesion 42, thereby promoting nucleation, and improving stress transfer. Glass 


 
 
transition temperatures, melting points, and crystallization behaviour were distinctly influenced 
by CF content, sizing, and chain extender. The group with no carbon fibre showed the lowest 
crystallinity. The lower crystallinity can be attributed to reduced crystalline regions when carbon 
fibres, the nucleating agent, are absent. When carbon fibres were added, the crystallization 
temperature (Tc) and initial crystallinity (Xc1) increased relative to the rPET3CE group. The 
effect was even more pronounced for groups containing sized carbon fibres. Notably, the 
groups with sized CF displayed higher crystallization temperatures (Tc) and crystallinity (Xc1), 
underscoring the role of sizing in promoting nucleation and enhancing polymer-fibre 
interactions. Figure 6 shows the DSC analysis of two groups, with and without sizing, where a 
noticeable shift in the heat flow curves is observed, leading to changes in enthalpy and, 
consequently, crystallinity. Interestingly, a small decrease in the second melting temperature 
(Tm2) was observed in groups with sized carbon fibres compared to rPET3CE. This decrease 
became more pronounced when the chain extender was added.  Although increased 
crystallinity can be an indicator of improved mechanical performance, there are other factors 
that collectively enhance the mechanical properties beyond what is achieved by crystallinity 
alone. The combined effect of CF sizing and chain extender is particularly noteworthy, as it 
demonstrated a synergistic influence on the material’s thermal and mechanical properties. 
While the chain extender slightly reduced crystallinity, its impact on the overall polymer 
structure, led to enhanced mechanical performance. The presence of chain extender improves 
fibre-matrix adhesion and acts as a physical crosslinker, specifically π–π stacking, improving 
the overall network structure of polymers. Both PET and the Nexamite have aromatic rings 43, 
which could result in a non-covalent interaction (orbital overlap) between the pi-bonds of the 
aromatic rings. This underscores the importance of balancing thermal and structural 
contributions when optimizing composite formulations. The reduced crystallinity in the absence 
of CF highlights its critical role as a nucleating agent. However, the presence of chain extender 
introduced nuanced effects, slightly reducing Tc and Xc1 in most cases, indicating that while 
chain extender improves fibre-matrix adhesion, it can slightly reduce the nucleating efficiency 
of carbon fibres. Despite this, the overall mechanical properties, particularly Young’s modulus, 
improved due to the enhanced polymer network structure facilitated by the chain extender. This 
highlights that although crystallinity plays an important role in determining the material's 
properties, the chain extender's effect on the polymer structure contributes significantly to 
overall performance, especially when combined with sized carbon fibres. Ultimately, the 
interplay between CF, sizing, and chain extender dictates not only the thermal behaviour but 
also the crystallinity and mechanical properties of the material. Among all the groups, carbon 
fibre sizing combined with additives appears to have a significant synergistic influence on the 
material's mechanical behaviour, which led to group rPET10sCF3CE outperforming the other 
groups in tensile modulus.

3.2. Mechanical characterisation of printed samples 
 
The tensile performance of FFF printed samples is listed in Table 5. A clear trend is observed 
in terms of tensile modulus: as the CF percentage increases, so does the modulus. This holds 
true both with and without chain extenders. Notably, literature indicates that the tensile modulus 
for recycled PET typically averages around 2.1 GPa26. However, with the incorporation of chain 
extenders, we achieved a tensile modulus exceeding 2.5 GPa, underscoring the efficacy of this 
approach. In this context, chain extenders like Nexamite increase the molecular weight of 
polymers, which can lead to improved mechanical performance. This effect is most evident in 
the groups with 10% CF, where the addition of chain extender appears to result in roughly a 
20% increase in tensile modulus. Referring to Figure 8, the groups with 10% CF and chain 
extender demonstrate the most significant improvement, with the modulus surpassing 7 GPa, 


 
 
highlighting the impact of both the fibres and chain extenders. It is noteworthy that, as reported 
by Katalagarianakis et al., their best-performing samples reached a tensile modulus of roughly 
4 GPa with 10% CF, while achieving over 6 GPa required 50% CF20. The influence of chain 
extender is not the sole factor in this equation; the outcome is rather an interplay between 
crystallinity and other material properties, such as the molecular orientation and the degree of 
fibre-matrix adhesion. Nexamite, as a chain extender, enhances fibre-matrix adhesion, and 
with lower CF content, this improvement in fibre-matrix bonding is less substantial. 
Consequently, the chain extender's potential to optimize the polymer network is limited, and 
the absence of significant reinforcement becomes the dominant factor. In such cases, the 
absence of reinforcement is more influential, mitigating the benefit of chain extenders. This 
observation aligns with the lower tensile modulus recorded for samples with lower CF content. 
During testing, most groups exhibited brittle failure, as shown in Figure 7, except for samples 
produced without reinforcement. The brittle failure mode correlated with the increased stiffness 
observed in groups with higher CF content. In contrast, samples with lower CF content 
displayed reduced stiffness, as indicated by their lower tensile modulus. This highlights the 
critical role of fibre reinforcement in dictating the mechanical behaviour of the printed parts. 
 
 
Figure 7: Brittle failure in a sample printed with a 10%CF filament after tensile testing 
 
The addition of CF not only enhanced the stiffness of printed samples, but also their strength 
especially in the presence of chain extender. By acting as a nucleating agent, the CF promotes 
the formation of crystalline regions, while the chain extender enhances the toughness of the 
amorphous regions. By combining the rigidity of crystalline regions with the toughness of 
amorphous regions, the enhanced polymer structure allows for a higher ultimate tensile 
strength. The optimization in the polymer network, combined with improved interfacial 
adhesion, allows for more effective load transfer and distribution. This is evident in Table 5, 
where the ultimate tensile strength of groups with CF and chain extenders shows an increase 
of over 20%. While fibres and sizing contribute to improvements, the predominant effect on the 
material's strength and stiffness stems from the chain-extenders. The addition of chain 
extender and hence its impact on the molar mass shows to be crucial in the production of 


 
 
printed parts with superior mechanical performance 44. The incorporation of chain extenders 
not only enhances fibre-matrix adhesion but also acts as a structural enhancer, improving the 
material’s ability to withstand mechanical loads. The results strongly indicate that the 
combination of CF and chain extender provides a significant advantage, offering an optimal 
balance between stiffness, strength, and toughness in rPET-based FFF parts.

3.3. Micro-CT 
 
To analyse the microstructural characteristics of the extruded filaments, X-ray micro-computed 
tomography (µCT) was employed, offering insight into the fibre orientation and length. Given 
the resource-intensive nature of micro-CT, the best-performing group with the highest CF 
content was chosen (rPET10sCF3CE). It is the group most likely to exhibit fibre misalignment 
and breakage, making it a representative sample of optimal properties. Segmentation and 
identification of fibres was used for processing of the images. A volume filter was applied, 
excluding volumes smaller than 100 µm³ and larger than 1500 µm³, to ensure that only volumes 
corresponding to the fibres were retained for analysis. For the length, two methods are used, 
including Principal Component Analysis (PCA)  45, and Bounding Box method (bb) 46. The PCA 
uses an eigenvector decomposition of the covariance matrix of each set of combined voxels. 
The covariance matrix is then used to approximate the set of voxels as an ellipsoid and the 
values of orientation, length etc., can be directly defined. The bb method simply encloses the 
set of voxels in a box and then defines the lengths as the sides of the box. The fibres from the 
images in a slice are seen below (axis red, green, blue are X, Y, Z, respectively). 
 
Figure 9: Image obtained from X-ray µCT scans of reinforced rPET filament, (a) showing the fibres 
inside a selected volume and (b) magnified view of the same volume, highlighting the orientation of 
the fibres. 
 
It can be seen that the resolution of the µCT scan is not adequate to visualize accurately 
potential inclusions on the surface of the fibres. It is evident that the fibres are well aligned 
along the X direction which is also visible in Figure 9. The length of the fibres is presented 
below for the bb and the PCA method. The resulting fibre probability distribution was plotted 
for the two methods (Figure 10), where the density represents the distribution of fibre lengths 
in relation to the total number of fibres analysed. The mean fibre length was found to be 86 to 
98 µm using bb and PCA, respectively. This distribution aligns closely with the data provided 
by Procotex, and the mean fibre length observed in our analysis is consistent with their 
specified fibre length of 100 µm in their data sheet 47. This suggests minimal to no breakage of 
the fibres during the process.

3.4. Fractography  
 
Tensile testing provided key insights into the mechanical behaviour of the samples under 
stress. However, a closer examination of the fracture surface is required to understand the 
underlying causes of fracture, as desired ductility originates from effective load transfer 
resulting from optimal fibre-matrix adhesion. Enhancing fibre-matrix interaction is a crucial 
approach to achieving strong and cohesive performance in composite materials. During tensile 
testing, the weak fibre-matrix interface disturbs the load transfer from the matrix to the fibres 
and leads to fibre pull-out. Consequently, since the fibres do not break, fibre pull-out leads to 
premature failure, preventing the fibres from reaching their full potential. To examine the 
fracture surface morphology and characterize fracture patterns, scanning electron microscopy 
was utilized. The chosen samples were from the groups with 10% CF with emphasis on the 
effect of fibre sizing and the effect of chain extender. Figures 11-A and 11-B depict 3D-printed 
samples with a 10% CF volume fraction, shown without fibre sizing and with fibre sizing, 
respectively.  The SEM images of the sample with unsized fibres shows evident fibre pull-out. 
The image reveals a distinct halo around the carbon fibres indicating weak interfacial bonding. 
Figure 11, A and B indicate that fibre sizing improves fibre-matrix adhesion. The reduction in 
fibre pull-out and voids indicates stronger fibre-matrix adhesion, which likely contributes to the 
improved mechanical properties observed in this particular group. Although the inclusion of 
fibre reinforcement in the matrix significantly improves the performance of a 3D-printed 
composite, the homogenization of the material is crucial to attain its full potential.  
 
Reprocessing and recycling PET often result in downcycling, as the material progressively 
loses its processability and its polymer microstructure gradually deteriorates 48.  The addition 
of chain extenders has shown to improve the viscosity by increasing average molecular weight 
of polyethylene terephthalate 21. Given its reactive nature, Nexamite was employed as a 
viscosity booster, aiming to enhance the bead microstructure and the melt flow, reducing the 
occurrence of voids and defects. This influence is evident in Figures 11-C and 12-D, where 
comparing samples with and without chain extender, showed that the addition of the viscosity 
booster results in significantly fewer voids and improved overall consistency. The improvement 
in melt flow and bead consistency is evident in the images, where the group with chain extender 
exhibits greater linearity and straighter bead formation.

Figure 12 highlights the importance of chain extenders, as demonstrated by the noticeable 
difference in this sample, without chain extender, compared to the previously shown group with 
chain extender in Figure 11-D. rPET5CF exhibited a lower tensile modulus, and in the 
magnified SEM image, tiny specks were visible across the beads in the printed sample. In the 
absence of chain extenders, these specks can be attributed to degraded particles during 
filament production. During thermal-oxidative degradation, the breakdown of macromolecular 
chains occurs. This leads to the generation of volatile substances such as acetaldehyde, along 
with the formation of linear and cyclic oligomers and trimmers, in addition to shorter 
macromolecules with carboxylic acid and vinyl ester end groups 49,50. These trimmers are 
shown in Figure 12.

Conclusion 
 
In this study, carbon fibre reinforced filaments were produced by incorporating up to 10% 
volume fraction of CF. The physio-chemical and mechanical properties were investigated with 
emphasis on the effect of carbon fibre, fibre sizing, and the addition of chain extenders. 
Produced by compounding and melt extrusion, feedstock filament composition with and without 
reinforcement were tested, using both sized and unsized fibres to provide a comprehensive 
overview of their behaviour. X-ray computed tomography scans were done to evaluate the fibre 
orientation and fibre-breakage, revealing satisfactory fibre alignment along the filament’s 
longitudinal axis, with minimal to no fibre breakage during extrusion. TGA and DSC were 
employed for thermal analysis. DSC measurements revealed that the addition of carbon fibres 
acted as nucleating agents, influencing the thermal stability and crystallization behaviour, while 
the chain extender also influenced these properties and improved adherence to the matrix 
surface. Most importantly, the tensile testing highlighted a substantial improvement in 
mechanical performance with the inclusion of carbon fibres and chain extenders. The 
increasing CF content improved the tensile properties, particularly in the groups that included 
the chain extender. The increase in CF content from 5% to 10% volume fraction yielded a more 
than 50% increase in tensile modulus. This superior tensile stiffness was most evident in 
groups containing sized CF and chain extenders. Notably, samples containing 10% sized CF 
and chain extenders exhibited a tensile modulus approximately double that of samples with 
5% unsized CF without chain extenders. SEM analysis further supported these findings, 
revealing distinct failure patterns at fracture surface level, along with improved fibre-matrix 
interfacial adhesion and reduced defects in the printed material. This study introduces a novel 
approach by synergistically combining fibre sizing and chain extenders in rPET composites. It 
highlights their critical role in not only enhancing tensile modulus but also improving the overall 
consistency and quality of extruded filaments. This approach presents a groundbreaking 
pathway for sustainable, high-performance additive manufacturing, addressing key challenges 
such as fibre integrity and fibre-matrix adhesion, which are often overlooked in studies. To 
adapt these findings for industrial applications, the methodology employed in this study 
provides a foundation for producing high-performance materials suitable for advanced 
manufacturing processes. By leveraging recycled materials and optimizing their mechanical 
properties, this work offers a pathway to integrate sustainable practices into the production of 
high-end products for industries such as automotive, aerospace, and consumer goods. Scaling 
these findings for industrial use would involve adapting extrusion and compounding processes 


 
 
to larger-scale equipment, ensuring consistent production while maintaining the enhanced 
properties of the materials. Future efforts could focus on refining extrusion techniques, 
exploring the compatibility of rPET composites with other reinforcing agents or additives, and 
testing these filaments under industrially relevant conditions, such as prolonged cyclic loading 
or impact applications. This direction aims to bridge the gap between laboratory-scale 
innovations and practical implementation in sustainable manufacturing processes, aligning 
with the growing need for eco-conscious industry practices.

Abstract: With the growing interest in sustainable manufacturing, 3D printing with recycled Polyethylene Terephthalate (rPET) offers an innovative approach to upcycling waste. This study explores the potential of combining rPET with milled short carbon fibres and polymer chain extenders to produce high-performance 3D printing filaments through melt extrusion. Filaments containing 5% and 10% carbon fibre, with and without sizing, along with a polymer chain extender, were investigated to enhance viscosity and material properties of rPET. Thermal analysis techniques evaluated the material's thermal stability and transitions, assessing the degradation temperature and calorimetric properties including glass transition and melting temperatures, while the measured carbon fibre content closely matched the theoretical content. Tensile testing of unidirectionally printed samples showed promising mechanical properties. X-ray micro-computed tomography assessed fibre length in extruded filaments, comparing it with the target length set during manufacturing, showing agreement. Scanning electron microscopy examined fracture and side surfaces, revealing governing failure mechanisms and defects, attributed to filament production and composition. This study highlights the synergistic role of carbon fibre sizing and chain extenders in enhancing tensile modulus, while improving overall consistency and quality of extruded filaments. It presents a groundbreaking pathway for sustainable, high-performance additive manufacturing.
